ai.definition: xAI is an advanced artificial intelligence methodology aimed at improving the transparency and reliability of machine learning models by enhancing their explainability.
ai.howItWorks: xAI employs techniques to make complex AI models more interpretable. This involves breaking down decision-making processes into understandable steps, allowing users to trace how inputs lead to outputs within a model.
ai.problemSolved: Lack of transparency and trust in AI systems, particularly in critical applications like healthcare or finance.
ai.manufacturing: xAI does not involve physical manufacturing but rather the development and refinement of algorithms and models.
ai.buildProcess: Involves training datasets with additional metadata to support interpretability, developing explainable AI frameworks, and validating model outputs through human-in-the-loop processes.
ai.costDrivers: High computational resources for training complex models; expertise in both AI and domain-specific knowledge required; validation and testing costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected to grow as trust in AI becomes increasingly important, especially in regulated industries.
ai.regulation: Varies by region but is expected to become more stringent with the increase in AI usage across critical sectors.
ai.risks: Dependence on accurate and representative training data; potential for oversimplification of complex models leading to loss of predictive power.
ai.profitability: Potentially high as it addresses a significant market need, but early-stage businesses may face challenges with adoption rates and regulatory compliance.
ai.futureDevelopment: Focus on integrating xAI techniques into existing AI pipelines, expanding application areas, and enhancing model robustness against adversarial attacks.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to computational demands during training but not in operation.

glossary.def: AI systems that provide clear and understandable reasons for their decisions or outputs.
The ability to understand the logic behind a model's predictions, making it easier to validate and trust its results.

subsystems.name: The model under study
subsystems.role: the opaque machine-learning system whose behaviour must be explained.
parts: inference interface exposing outputs, and where possible gradients and internal activations

subsystems.name: Attribution methods
subsystems.role: estimate how much each input feature contributed to a given output.
parts: surrogate models fitted locally around one prediction

subsystems.name: Concept and representation probes
subsystems.role: look inside the network rather than only at its inputs and outputs.
parts: probe classifiers trained on hidden activations
circuit analysis tracing which components drive a behaviour

subsystems.name: Example-based explanations
subsystems.role: explain a decision by comparison with real or synthetic cases.

subsystems.name: Faithfulness evaluation
subsystems.role: tests whether an explanation actually reflects the model, not just looks plausible.

subsystems.name: Human interface and governance
subsystems.role: turns scores into something a person can act on and audit.

buildSteps.title: Define the question
buildSteps.detail: Decide exactly what must be explained — one prediction, overall model behaviour, a subgroup, or a suspected failure mode — because the answer determines which method is valid.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the model
buildSteps.detail: Expose outputs, gradients and selected internal activations through an inference wrapper so explanation code can query the model repeatedly without retraining it.

buildSteps.title: Pick a method class
buildSteps.detail: Choose attribution, probe-based or example-based approaches according to whether inputs, internals or training data are accessible, and how much compute is acceptable.

buildSteps.title: Generate explanations
buildSteps.detail: Run the chosen estimator over the model — often thousands of forward passes per explanation — and aggregate the results into per-feature, per-concept or per-example scores.

buildSteps.title: Validate faithfulness
buildSteps.detail: Test explanations against the model itself: remove the features they mark as important and check the output actually moves, and confirm that randomising the model changes the explanation.

buildSteps.title: Check human usefulness
buildSteps.detail: Have domain experts use the explanations on real decisions and measure whether they detect errors or change their judgement appropriately.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Serve explanations alongside predictions, document the method's known limits, and re-run validation whenever the model or its data distribution changes.

prerequisites.why: explanation methods need repeated access to outputs, gradients or activations.
methods such as additive feature-attribution estimators and activation probes are mature and widely implemented.

prerequisites.tech: Ground-truth or causally valid test data
prerequisites.why: faithfulness is easy to measure on synthetic tasks and much harder on real-world models.
there is no settled standard for comparing explanations across models and tasks.
many methods require thousands of extra forward passes per explanation.

pathway.milestone: post-hoc attribution and documentation routinely shipped with models
pathway.unlocks: debugging, regulatory reporting and basic user trust.

pathway.milestone: concept-based and circuit-level interpretability on frontier models
pathway.unlocks: explanations that describe internal features rather than only input importance.

pathway.milestone: standardised faithfulness benchmarks and third-party audits
pathway.unlocks: comparable, testable claims about model transparency.

pathway.milestone: interpretability that reliably predicts behaviour before deployment
pathway.unlocks: safety cases that rest on understanding a model, not only on testing it.
